reason: The text presents and emphasizes a clear, multi-tiered hierarchical structure throughout. Pharaoh stands at the apex, followed by his officials (Potiphar, chief jailer), then Joseph in positions of authority over subordinates and prisoners. The narrative repeatedly reinforces hierarchy through: (1) Joseph's elevation through successive hierarchical positions (household overseer, then prison administrator); (2) explicit statements of delegated authority ('all that he had, he gave into Joseph's hand'); (3) Joseph's moral reasoning against violating hierarchy (his refusal of Potiphar's wife emphasizes respect for his master's authority and even higher divine authority); (4) the proper functioning of the system through established chains of command. While the text doesn't philosophically advocate for hierarchy in the abstract, it implicitly encourages respect for hierarchical structures by presenting Joseph's conduct within them as morally praiseworthy and rewarded by divine blessing.
